newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Croats open fire on Mostar Moslems, four wounded.
newsitem.headline: Croats open fire on Mostar Moslems, four wounded.

text.p: Bosnian Croats opened fire on a crowd of Moslems visiting a cemetery in the divided town of Mostar on Monday, wounding at least four people, an international police spokesman said.
"A group of Croats opened fire on the group visiting the cemetery. We have an initial report of four casualties," Alexander Ivanko told Reuters.
The NATO-led peace force said three were seriously wounded and one person was slightly injured by gunfire. Other Moslems in the procession were injured by stones thrown by the Croat mob.
Witnesses said some 100 Croats tried to stop the Moslems from entering the Liska cemetery, where Croat and Moslem war dead are buried side by side.
The mob began beating some of the Moslems and then shots rang out, spreading panic among the crowd, said Alija Behram, a radio journalist from the Moslem-controlled eastern sector.
"A guy close to me was shot in the forehead," Behram told Reuters by telephone afterwards. "There was panic all around us. There were 10 to 15 people wounded."
Behram said the man shot in the head died from his wounds.
There was no independent confirmation of the casualty toll from local hospitals.
Behram said he saw an Islamic cleric who led the procession, Mufti Hadziseid Efendija Smajkic, being taken to hospital for gunshot wounds to his legs.
Several men in the Croat mob were wearing blue police uniforms and about 20 civilians were carrying sticks. Another witness alleged some of the Croats were armed with rifles.

The NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) and international police monitors later reported that a group of Croat men -- possibly armed -- had gathered near a former front line in front of the Hotel Ero.
Another group of Moslem men, possibly armed, had gathered at a nearby bridge in the Moslem-held eastern sector.

The Sarajevo-based BH press agency reported that several thousand Moslems had participated in the procession. Monday was the second day of the Islamic religious holiday of Bairam, when Moslems mourn their dead.
Spanish peacekeeping troops were patrolling the streets in armoured vehicles to try to defuse tensions between rival Croat and Moslem communities.
Ivanko said U.N. police monitors were still investigating the shooting incident which occurred at about 2 p.m. (1300 GMT) in the town centre near a former front line.
The shooting follows rising tensions over the past month in Mostar between rival Moslem and Croat communities.
Two major explosions were reported overnight and armed Croat men expelled Moslems from their flat in Croat-controlled west Mostar on Sunday, Ivanko said.
The violence has coincided with political battles inside the Moslem-Croat federation over power-sharing and budgets.
Bosnian Moslems and Croats fought a vicious 10-month war in 1993-94 until agreeing to form the federation under heavy U.S. pressure.
Croat hardline nationalists in western Mostar have refused to submit to federation authority and blocked efforts at reunifying the town.
A newly-elected Croat-Moslem government has no offices because Croat hardliners have occupied a building which is supposed to house the city administration.
